# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
This comment has two parts that need separating. Sections 1–5 are a valuable re-analysis that uses the microdata to confirm, with numbers, most of the concerns raised about the Halden paper. Sections 6–8 go well beyond that evidence. The headline conclusion that the per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the randomised trial the comment itself cites.

## The arithmetic

The figures in Table 2 are correct:
- 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%
- 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%
- 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%

The hours ratios match (34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861). The real revenue figure is also correct: 1.014/1.041 ≈ −2.6%.

There are two numerical problems:

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Section 3 says the actual-hours shortfall comes from +0.7 hours a day on four days (2.8 h) plus 1.6 h logged on the day off. That gives 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = **36.4** hours a week, not the reported **34.6**. To reach 34.6, the extra time must total about 2.6 h. Even the per-day figure alone (2.8 h) exceeds that. Either the decomposition or the average is wrong. This matters because the 14.1% figure drives the hours correction.

**The novelty extrapolation is off.** A straight line through 0.61 SD at month 3 and 0.29 SD at month 6 reaches zero at about month **8.7**, not "around month ten." The bigger problem is with the method, which I cover under issue 2.

## Main issues

**1. The paper's own cited evidence contradicts its conclusion.**
The comment calls the Varden counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." That trial's other stratum is just as rigorous: case-processing offices had randomisation, administrative records, timesheet hours, and nine months of follow-up. It found output per actual hour **+12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**, and that design addresses each of the comment's four problems:

- **Selection:** offices were randomised, and none withdrew.
- **Output measurement:** output came from administrative records, not managers.
- **Hours:** the denominator was actual hours, not scheduled hours.
- **Novelty:** follow-up was nine months, and control staff also knew a trial was running.

Varden has its own weaknesses: few clusters, possibly unclaimed overtime, and the possibility that cutting meetings drives much of the gain. These might shrink the estimate, but they don't make it an artifact. Using Varden's negative stratum while ignoring its positive one is selective. A defensible conclusion would say that per-hour gains in the uncontrolled pilots are heavily inflated, and that the best randomised evidence suggests a real but smaller gain in work not tied to presence.

**2. The novelty argument is a hypothesis, not a correction.**
- **The energy data have weaknesses.** Self-reported energy is not output. A straight line through two points can't show where the trend ends; a plateau fits the data equally well. And on the comment's own extrapolation, energy would return to baseline around month 9, yet Varden still found per-hour gains at month 9.
- **The microdata contain a direct test that the comment doesn't run.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*. If novelty drives the gain, output (or output per hour) in the record-based subset should decline from month 1 to month 6. Running this check would carry far more weight than an extrapolation from energy scores.
- **The burden of proof runs both ways.** "Entirely an artifact" is an affirmative claim. A measured residual of +10.8% is not removed by asserting that it is probably novelty.

**3. Attrition is listed as corrected, but it isn't.**
The abstract says the gain falls to 10.8% after "correcting the first three" problems, which include attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The attrition finding itself is important: the Halden paper says the nine withdrawals happened in the preparation phase, but the microdata say seven occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons. This looks like a factual misstatement in the original, and the Halden authors should answer it. Two additions would quantify it:

- **Bounding.** Assign the withdrawn organisations pessimistic outcomes, for example output at 80 (zero per-hour gain) or at the worst observed level. This shows how much survivorship could move the estimate.
- **Continuation.** Counting withdrawals as non-continuers, continuation falls from 56/61 (92%) to 56/70 (80%). That is still high, but noticeably less striking.

**4. The record-based output measure may be biased downward in some organisations.**
The listed record types include **billable hours delivered**. In a reduced-hours trial, billable hours are almost an input measure: if staff work fewer hours, billable hours fall almost by definition. Organisations that measured output this way will show output falling with hours regardless of real productivity. The comment should report results by record type, or exclude billable-hours organisations as a sensitivity check.

Beyond that, the 19-of-23 pattern is strong evidence of manager overstatement (sign test, one-sided p ≈ 0.001). It would help to state whether Table 1 uses employee weights, as Halden did.

**5. The abstract and conclusion disagree with each other, and with the Data note.**
- The abstract says the four problems account for "**most**" of the gain, and then concludes "**entirely**."
- Revenue is one of the four problems, but it doesn't enter the per-hour calculation at all, so it can't account for any of the gain.
- The Data note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The Conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
- Table 2 is described as "successive corrections," but each row uses a different subset (61, 23, 27, 17). The rows are separate estimates, not a decomposition of one gain. The comment should report manager-reported output and scheduled-hours gains for the 17-organisation subset too, so that the size of each correction can be seen within one sample.

## Section 7 mischaracterises the Varden paper

- The Varden authors did not present meetings as an established mechanism. They called the analysis unregistered and based on seven offices, said it "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's objection largely repeats their own caveats.
- "Selected for analysis after the results were known" appears to be wrong. The meetings data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- The hypothesis also has independent support. In the Halden manager interviews, 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings.
- Most importantly, if fewer meetings explain the gain, the gain is real, not an artifact. The correct implication is that the hours cut may not be what causes the gain, which is a different and more interesting claim.

## Smaller points

- **Revenue.** CPI is an approximate deflator for business revenue; sector producer prices would be better. The comment's broader point is right: a 1.4% nominal rise during 4% inflation is not evidence of growth.
- **Retail.** The fall of 11.2% for "three retail and hospitality organisations" rests on n = 3 and should be presented as indicative only. Comparing it with Varden is reasonable, since both point to coverage-bound work.

## Strengths worth keeping

- The attrition finding.
- The comparison of manager-reported and record-based output.
- Using logged hours.
- The point about the per-hour metric across sectors.
- The candid Data note.
- The recommendations, especially analysing all enrolled organisations and following up for 18 months or more.

If Sections 6–8 were scaled back to match this evidence, the comment would be a strong contribution.

## How the three papers fit together

| | Halden (original) | Varga & Holm (re-analysis) | Varden (RCT) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, non-coverage work | +23.4% | +10.8% (subset of 17) | +12.5% (case-processing) |
| Coverage-bound work | "Gains everywhere" | Output falls | Output per employee −11.4% |

The two corrected estimates converge on roughly a 10–13% per-hour gain in work not tied to presence. That convergence argues against "entirely an artifact." Each estimate has its own possible downward corrections: novelty in Halden, and few clusters and unclaimed overtime in Varden. Whether the gain is durable, and whether it comes from shorter hours or from the reorganisation that shorter hours prompted, remains open. The Varden 24-month follow-up is the best placed to answer both.

I can draft this as a referee report for the journal, or as a short reply on behalf of either set of authors, if useful.
